Package me.bristermitten.mittenlib.annotations.ast

@NullMarked package me.bristermitten.mittenlib.annotations.ast
The structure of a config's data in a more abstract form than a class hierarchy.

As a reference, there are 3 ways of organising data for a config. The first, most simple, is an atomic structure, described by a simple class or interface, eg: 


 @Config public interface TestConfig {
 int number();
 }

We can then compose config types into bigger ones using inheritance, creating an intersection structure: 

     @Config
     public interface AddedConfig extends TestConfig {
         int anotherNumber();
     }

This describes a structure with 2 properties, the int number and the int anotherNumber. When using interfaces, multiple inheritance is allowed for more flexible composition. Note that the actual implementation (composition vs inheritance) is left as an implementation detail. Finally, we can create a union of types: 


 import me.bristermitten.mittenlib.config.Config;
 import org.jspecify.annotations.Nullable;
     @ConfigUnion
     public interface RepositoryConfig {
         @Config
         interface URLConfig extends RepositoryConfig {
             String url();

             @Nullable String authToken();
         }

         @Config
         interface FileSystemConfig extends RepositoryConfig {
             String path();
         }
     }

which essentially says that anytime a RepositoryConfig is referenced, it can be in the form of either of the subtypes. Note that this is an undiscriminated union, i.e. there's nothing to distinguish between the two subtypes aside from their structure. This is not considered a design flaw, but it means there's often no fast way to deserialise aside from trial and error.
